comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

Strongly in favour, and I think the value is different from the one in the proposal.

The proposal frames it as *more eval data*. The bigger win is **distribution**. Our synthetic eval set is generated from a fact graph, so its questions are uniformly well-formed: complete sentences, correct entity names, unambiguous intent. Real cohort questions are none of those. They have typos, missing context, two questions in one, and pronouns with no antecedent.

A retriever tuned on well-formed questions and deployed against real ones degrades in ways the synthetic set cannot show you. **The replay slice is valuable precisely because it is messy**, and that should be the headline argument rather than the sample count.

replies.body:
> **Noor** · cohort peer · works in a regulated bank

Adding the constraint that will decide whether this is buildable: if you replay real questions you are handling real user data, and in my industry that needs consent and a retention policy before the first question is stored.

Not an objection — a design requirement. Anonymise at capture, not later; store the question text and nothing that identifies who asked it; and put a TTL on the slice. It is much easier to build this correctly than to retrofit it.

Both right, and Noor's point promotes this from an idea to something with a design. Capturing the shape:

- **Value** is distributional realism, not volume — that is the sentence that goes in the issue.
- **Capture** anonymises at write time; question text only; TTL enforced.
- **Labelling** is the cost nobody has priced. Real questions have no gold evidence, so somebody has to label them, and that is the work. Probably a small hand-labelled slice rather than the whole stream.
- **Open question worth its own thread:** if the replay slice disagrees with the synthetic slice, which one gates a release? I do not think the answer is obvious and I would rather argue it before we have the data than after.
